text: Thurgood Marshall and Loren Miller argued for the families.
On the third of May, 1948, the Supreme Court ruled in Shelley versus Kraemer.
The decision was clever and limited at once.
A covenant between private people, the Court said, was not itself against the Constitution.
But the moment a court enforced one, the government became the enforcer, and the Fourteenth Amendment forbids the government from discriminating that way.
So the clauses could no longer be enforced.
It was a real victory, and Black families across the country began to cross the old lines.
But notice what the Court did not do.
It did not strike the covenants from the deeds.
It did not ban redlining.
It did not touch the FHA manual.
It pulled one tool out of the toolbox and left the rest on the bench.
They could still be written.
And they were.
For years afterward the racist language sat in millions of American deeds, including thousands here in Chicago, legally dead but never erased.
You can still order a copy of your deed today and find it there, a sentence that no longer has teeth but never had to apologize.
Illinois did not give homeowners a way to formally strike that language from the record until 2022.
And the lines drawn in the 1930s did not fade when the law changed.
Researchers who lay the old HOLC maps over the cities of today find the red zones still poorer, still sicker, still hotter in summer, with less tree cover and shorter lives.
The wall came down.
The shadow it cast did not.
That is the shape of this harm.
It rarely shouted.
It was a table in a book, a manual in a file drawer, a color on a map, a line in a deed.
Quiet, official, and built to last.
